paragraphs: A major theme in "The Necklace" is that excessive pride and the fear of confessing the truth can lead to unnecessary ruin. Instead of being honest about losing the jewelry, Mathilde Loisel spends ten grueling years doing hard labor to replace it, which completely strips away her youth and beauty. The ending strongly develops this theme when Mathilde finally talks to her old friend and Madame Forestier reveals the shocking truth: “Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!” This ironic moment proves the narrator's reflection that "How small a thing is needed to make or ruin us!" because Mathilde destroyed her entire life to replace an imitation piece simply because she was too proud to admit an accident. In real life, people often face a similar dilemma when they make a mistake and try to cover it up instead of telling the truth, usually ending up in far worse trouble than if they had just been honest in the first place.

The text is The Necklace by Guy de Maupassant. A major theme in the story are that pride and hiding the truth causes pointless misery. Mathilde loses the diamond necklace at the ball, she decides to secretly replace it instead of confessing. Her and her husband works for ten years in terrible poverty to pay off the massive debt. Because she was too proud to admit her mistake. By the time the debt is paid, Mathilde is completely ruined because "She had become the woman of impoverished households—strong and hard and rough." The ending develops the theme when Mathilde meets Madame Forestier again it reveals that all her suffering was useless. Her friend reveals the shocking truth when she says, "Oh, my poor Mathilde! Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!" In real life, people often buys luxury items they cannot afford just to look rich on social media. Just like Mathilde, they end up trapped in debt and stress all because they cared too much about what other people thought.

In the story "The Necklace," a main theme is that Mathilde loses a diamond necklace after a fancy party and has to work for ten years to pay off all the debt. The surprise ending develops the lesson about pride because she finally finds out the truth after wasting her entire youth. The author explains, "She washed the dishes, using her dainty fingers and rosy nails on greasy pots and pans." This shows that her hands got ruined from doing the chores, which clearly proves that people should always tell the truth right away instead of being scared. Because she hid what happened, Mathilde had to live a more harder life than she ever expected just to replace the jewelry. At the very end, Madame Forestier reveals the secret when she says, "Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!" This quote shows that the necklace was only worth five hundred francs and was fake, which proves that Madame Forestier was trying to trick Mathilde from the beginning. In real life, people experience this kind of situation when they pretend to be rich or popular on social media to impress their peers, but trying to keep up that fake image usually ends up causing a lot of regret.

In Guy de Maupassant's short story "The Necklace," a major theme is that false pride and trying to protect an expensive reputation can ruin a person's entire life. The shocking ending develops this theme because Mathilde loses her youth and freedom over an object that was not even genuine. After the necklace goes missing, she enters extreme poverty and endures "the odious cares of the kitchen," which shows how she became very hateful and malicious while performing daily household chores. She lost all her beauty. Mathilde also ruined her life over simple pride, and when she meets her friend years later, she smiles with a look that is "at once proud and ingenuous," which proves she had a lot of ingenuity and clever tricks to pay off the massive loans. However, the ending proves her sacrifice was completely useless when Madame Forestier cries, "Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!" which reveals the necklace was just made out of cheap craft glue. People do this in high school too. In real life, people often pretend to have fancy clothes or hide their blunders because they are terrified of looking poor, but hiding the truth to save their social status only leads to years of pointless stress and regret.

A major theme in "The Necklace" is that letting pride prevent honesty can cause unnecessary suffering and ruin a person's life. Throughout the excerpt, Mathilde Loisel endures a decade of grueling poverty simply because she was too ashamed to admit to her wealthy friend that she had lost the borrowed jewelry. Instead of telling the truth, she faces the "horrible existence of the needy" and transforms from an admired beauty into a woman who is "strong and hard and rough" just to repay the enormous loan for a real diamond necklace. The ending strongly reinforces this theme through dramatic irony when Madame Forestier reveals, "Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!" This shocking twist shows that Mathilde completely sacrificed her youth and happiness over an imitation, proving that her excessive pride was her true downfall. In real life, people often fall into the same trap when they make a simple mistake—like accidentally breaking a friend's possession or lying about a bad grade—and choose to hide it out of fear of judgment. While covering up the truth might protect someone's ego in the short term, the guilt, stress, and consequences of the deception almost always end up being far worse than just being honest from the beginning.

A major theme in Guy de Maupassant's "The Necklace" is that excessive pride and the fear of being honest can turn a minor mistake into a lifetime of unnecessary ruin. At the end of the story, this theme is powerfully developed through dramatic irony when Madame Loisel finally confesses that she spent a decade doing brutal physical labor to replace the lost diamonds. Instead of being impressed by her sacrifice, Madame Forestier is horrified and reveals the truth, exclaiming, "Why, my necklace was paste! It was worth at most only five hundred francs!" Mathilde's refusal to admit the truth right away cost her youth and happiness, leaving her where "Madame Loisel looked old now" and had transformed into "the woman of impoverished households—strong and hard and rough." This situation connects to real life because people often dig themselves into deeper holes just to protect their pride or reputation. For example, teenagers might hide a bad grade or cover up a minor car dent out of embarrassment, only to face far worse consequences and stress when the truth eventually comes out, proving that honesty is always better than living a costly lie.
